title: Virtual Triage A
subtitle: 8-month-old with respiratory distress
stem: It is 7:40 pm in the paediatric emergency room. A mother hurries in carrying her 8-month-old daughter. You are the triage nurse.
parent: "Sister, she has had a cold and cough for three days. Since this afternoon she is breathing very fast and she won't take the breast. She feels hot."

vitals.note: Irritable but consolable in mother's arms. Nasal flaring, subcostal and intercostal recessions, audible wheeze. Pink lips, warm hands. Room air.

decisions.title: Impression
decisions.prompt: From the doorway: irritable but consolable on her mother, good tone, looking at you; breathing fast with flaring, recessions and wheeze; pink, no mottling. What is your impression — stable or unstable, life-threatening or not, and which system is affected?
decisions.key: Unstable, non-life-threatening; breathing affected — respiratory distress.

options.text: Stable — a well infant with a cough; she can wait in the routine queue
options.outcome: You send her to the waiting queue. Twelve minutes later her mother rushes back: she has stopped crying and is breathing faster. SpO₂ 87 %, RR 66.
options.note: Two sides of the PAT are abnormal. Increased work of breathing with flaring and recessions is never "stable"; this child must not wait in the routine queue.

options.text: Unstable, non-life-threatening — breathing affected: respiratory distress
options.outcome: You take her straight past the queue to the triage bed, keep her upright on her mother’s lap and attach the monitor.
options.note: Unstable but not yet life-threatening: appearance is normal (consolable, good tone, interactive) while work of breathing is increased — respiratory distress, lower airway (wheeze). The infant is compensating, and compensation can be lost quickly at 8 months, so she needs treatment now and close watching.

options.text: Unstable, life-threatening — respiratory failure; start bag-mask ventilation
options.outcome: You call the resuscitation team and reach for the bag and mask. She is awake, consolable and fighting the mask; her chest is moving well. The team asks why she is being bagged.
options.note: In respiratory failure appearance is abnormal: lethargy, poor tone, not interacting, or a slowing or silent chest. She is irritable but consolable and interactive. Over-calling failure wastes the resuscitation bay; under-calling distress is the greater danger — reassess every few minutes.

options.text: Unstable — circulation affected: shock, because the heart rate is 168
options.outcome: You ask for an IV line and a fluid bolus. While the trolley is prepared nobody attends to her breathing; the recessions are deeper.
options.note: Tachycardia alone is not shock. Her circulation-to-skin side is normal: pink, warm, CRT 2 s. Fever, distress and crying all raise the heart rate. Shock needs abnormal circulation signs: pallor, mottling, cool extremities, delayed CRT.

must: respiratory distress or breathing affected (a nurse who names respiratory distress meets this; she need not write the words stable/unstable)

decisions.title: Intervention
decisions.prompt: She is unstable with respiratory distress and wheeze, SpO₂ 89 % on room air. What is your intervention?
decisions.key: Start oxygen — any form is acceptable (nasal prongs, face mask, non-rebreather) — titrated to SpO₂ 94–98 %, and prepare nebulisation (salbutamol, oxygen-driven at 6–8 L/min).

options.text: Start oxygen (any device) titrated to SpO₂ 94–98 % and prepare a salbutamol nebulisation
options.outcome: Oxygen on; she settles on her mother’s lap. SpO₂ rises to 95 %, RR 56, HR 160. The salbutamol nebuliser is drawn up and ready, to be driven with oxygen at 6–8 L/min.
options.note: Oxygen first, by whatever device she tolerates, to a target of 94–98 %; then treat the wheeze — prepare an oxygen-driven salbutamol nebulisation. Reassess within minutes.

options.text: Start oxygen only, and keep watching
options.outcome: SpO₂ creeps up to 94 %, but the wheeze and recessions are unchanged and she is still breathing at 62 a minute.
options.note: Oxygen treats the hypoxaemia, not the bronchospasm. With a wheeze, prepare the nebuliser at the same time.

options.text: Give a salbutamol nebulisation with room air or a compressor, without oxygen
options.outcome: The nebuliser hisses on a compressor. SpO₂ drifts down to 86 % and her heart rate climbs to 174.
options.note: A hypoxaemic child should be nebulised with oxygen (6–8 L/min), never with air; salbutamol can briefly worsen ventilation–perfusion mismatch.

options.text: Secure an IV line and send bloods first
options.outcome: Two attempts at a cannula. She screams and struggles: RR 70, HR 176, the recessions deepen.
options.note: An IV is not an A or B intervention, and the struggle will worsen her breathing. Nothing here needs IV access yet.

options.text: No oxygen yet — observe for 15 minutes and recheck
options.outcome: Fifteen minutes later she is tiring: SpO₂ 86 %, HR 174, the cry is weaker.
options.note: SpO₂ 89 % with increased work of breathing is below the target of 94–98 %. Start oxygen now; observing does not treat hypoxaemia and the infant is tiring.

decisions.title: Triage category
decisions.prompt: On oxygen her SpO₂ is 95 %, RR 56, HR 160, still recessing. Which triage level, and what does it mean for her?

options.text: Level 1 · Resuscitation — straight to the resuscitation bay, call the team
options.outcome: The resuscitation team gathers round a pink, alert infant on oxygen. Five minutes later an ambulance brings in a child in arrest — and the only resuscitation bay is occupied.
options.note: Level 1 is for failure or arrest: apnoea, silent chest, unresponsive, hypotensive shock. She responded to oxygen and is still compensating. Over-triage here blocks the bay for the next child who needs it; the right answer is Level 2 with the doctor at the bedside in minutes.

options.text: Level 2 · Emergent — doctor to see within 10 minutes, continuous monitoring, nurse stays with her
options.outcome: She stays on the monitored triage bed with you beside her: continuous SpO₂ and heart rate, reassessed every 5 minutes.
options.note: Respiratory distress needing oxygen is Level 2: continuous SpO₂ and heart-rate monitoring, reassess every 5 minutes, escalate immediately if she tires. She does not leave your sight.

options.text: Level 4 · Less urgent — she is pink on oxygen, she can wait her turn
options.outcome: She goes back to the waiting area on a portable cylinder. Twenty minutes later SpO₂ is 90 % and RR 64; the recessions are deeper.
options.note: A pink SpO₂ on oxygen does not make her less urgent; it means the oxygen is working for now. The work of breathing is unchanged and infants tire without warning. Level 4 means she could wait an hour unmonitored.

options.text: Level 5 · Non-urgent — give a nebuliser and send to the OPD queue
options.outcome: Her mother carries her to the OPD queue. Thirty minutes later she is rushed back: grey, RR 68, SpO₂ 86 %, HR 178.
options.note: An infant on oxygen for respiratory distress is not an outpatient. This is the triage decision that leads to a collapse in the waiting area.

decisions.title: ISBAR call to the doctor
decisions.prompt: You phone the paediatric registrar. Which handover gets the doctor to the bedside fastest, with the right picture?

options.text: "Doctor, there's a baby here with a cough and fever, can you come when you're free?"
options.outcome: "I'll come when I finish here." Thirty minutes pass and the registrar has not arrived.
options.note: No identification, no situation, no objective data, no request with a timeframe. "When you're free" invites a 40-minute wait.

options.text: "Doctor, this is Sister Rani in triage. I have an 8-month-old, 8 kg, in respiratory distress: RR 62, SpO₂ 89 % on air, now 95 % on 2 L nasal prongs, HR 160, wheeze both sides, recessions, Temp 38.2. I've triaged her Level 2. I need you at the bedside within 10 minutes."
options.outcome: The registrar repeats the numbers back and says she is on her way. She is at the bedside in six minutes.
options.note: ISBAR: Identify yourself and the patient, Situation in one line, Background and Assessment with numbers, and a Recommendation with a timeframe. The doctor can picture the child before arriving.

options.text: "Doctor, bed 3, 8 months, looks like bronchiolitis, I've started oxygen, see her after the ward round."
options.outcome: The registrar finishes the ward round first. Fifty minutes pass before she arrives.
options.note: A diagnosis is offered but no vital signs, no request and no timeframe. "After the ward round" could be an hour. State the numbers and what you need.

options.text: Send a WhatsApp message with the vitals to the on-call group and continue monitoring
options.outcome: The message shows two grey ticks. Twenty-five minutes later nobody has replied.
options.note: A Level 2 child needs a closed-loop call: you speak, the doctor confirms they are coming and when. A group message may not be read.

debrief: What was your impression, and which findings made her unstable but not yet life-threatening?
At which point would you have upgraded her to Level 1? Name three signs.
What would you check at each 5-minute reassessment while waiting for the doctor?
takeHome: Impression first: stable or unstable, life-threatening or not, and which system — here, unstable non-life-threatening respiratory distress.
Intervention: oxygen by any device to SpO₂ 94–98 %, and prepare an oxygen-driven salbutamol nebulisation for the wheeze.
Distress on oxygen is Level 2, never Level 4: monitored, reassessed every 5 minutes.
ISBAR with numbers and a timeframe gets the doctor to the bed.
references: AHA PALS Provider Manual 2020: Pediatric Assessment Triangle, respiratory distress and failure, oxygen therapy.
IAP ICC PCCN Module 01: PAT, ABCDE, triage levels, DIRECT approach.

ending.smooth: The registrar confirms bronchiolitis and admits her to the HDU on nasal prongs. By the next morning she is feeding at the breast and the recessions are settling.
ending.detour: She reaches the doctor and the HDU, but the detours meant a longer spell of hypoxaemia and a tiring infant; she needed high-flow oxygen on admission.
